claims.claim: docs/README.md defines the vocabulary: source table (the Float32Array a program reads), cell (one number of it: constant, input, event bit or state), wire, operation, builder function, evaluation (one run), and host (the JavaScript around the program).

An event cell is an exact bit JavaScript sets to 1 and the program resets to 0; nextSource lists each cell's next-value wire (constants and inputs hold themselves, events hold 0), and a state cell with zero or two next values throws while building.

The template toggle acts on release: a press on the track arms it, a release on the track while armed flips it, and the thumb springs 20 px to its new side; it has 20 cells (viewport 2, two pointer events with x and y, cancel, on, armed, 4 spring-matrix cells, settleCheck, snap, thumb displacement, velocity, destination).

State lives in source-table cells: each state cell has exactly one next-value wire, and the host copies next values back after an evaluation (source.set(result.nextValues)); iteration happens across evaluations.

There are exactly four instruction kinds, AtomKind = 'affine' | 'reglu' | 'boolean' | 'index': affine(left) = left; reglu(left, gate) = f(left × max(0, gate)); boolean(score) = f(f(f(score) + 8,388,609) − 8,388,609); index reads values[candidates[floor(form)]].

Every arithmetic step rounds to FP32 like Math.fround, and a weighted sum is evaluated term by term in stored order: value = f(bias); then value = f(value + f(f(coefficient) × values[wire])) for each term.

The README's '2 primitives' (matrix multiplication + reglu) and the runtime's four instructions are compatible: affine is the matmul, reglu the nonlinearity, the boolean atom an optional FP32 shortcut, and the index read a copy that replaces a one-hot masked sum.
FP32 holds every integer exactly only up to 2^24 = 16,777,216; Math.fround(2^24 + 1) = 16,777,216 and Math.fround(2^24 + 3) = 16,777,220.

The runtime does not ship the README line literally: emitCompare picks integer bits when both operands lie on grids within 2^24 grid steps (a constant like 4 gets a grid automatically), otherwise a sign cascade; it throws without finite declared ranges.

On a grid, a > b is built as relu(1 − relu(1 − D)) with D = (a − b)/grid; for a > 4 with assumeGrid(a, 1) that is ramp = relu(5 − a) then bit = relu(1 − ramp): 2 operations in 2 layers. It equals the README ramp at every integer and ends in a ReGLU product so readers cannot copy large ReLU values into their sums.

Declarations (assumeRange, assumeGrid with a power-of-two step, assumeOneHot, assumeBit) let the builder pick cheap exact constructions; they are promises, checked by validators in tests (validateGrids, validateIndexReads, validateOneHotGroups), and a declaration after a reader exists throws.

claims.claim: Without a grid the bit for a > 4 (a within −1000..1000) is a sign cascade of 16 operations in 15 layers: d = f(a − 4) kept as its own operation, six clamp stages scaling by 2^14 then 2^24 five times, then the final ReGLU relu(1 − 2^15 · stage) and bit = relu(1 − that); the scales multiply to 2^149, and a = 4.5 gives the correct bit 1.

The sign cascade works because subnormals make f(a − b) zero only when a === b; power-of-two scaling only changes the exponent, so stages lift any nonzero difference down to 2^-149 to at least 1. Row heights 229, 167.4, 208.5 and 194.4 px sum to 799.300048828125 as a loop and 799.2999877929688 in pairs, one FP32 step (2^-14) apart.

On the CPU executor, the tree takes longer than the loop with either network (knuth-plass's tree 1.7-7.7× its chain's time); a GPU, where one level is one dispatch, is where a tree can win (knuth-plass 0.47 ms on WebGPU against 3.4 ms for the chain on the CPU).

The index read is one instruction at any table size: over 10,000 entries a ReLU one-hot masked sum compiles to 30,002 live operations and 49,998 stored weights with gather lowering, against 1 operation and 1 stored weight.

There are exactly four instruction kinds, AtomKind = 'affine' | 'reglu' | 'boolean' | 'index': affine(left) = left; reglu(left, gate) = f(left × max(0, gate)); boolean(score) = f(f(f(score) + 8,388,609) − 8,388,609); index reads values[candidates[floor(form)]].

Per pattern after a pause: error 12.0 ms vs RegExp 20.8 ms; [a-z]+Id 11.6 vs 19.3; the date pattern 13.1 vs 8.9 (RegExp wins); ([a-z]+)+x 11.0 ms vs 2.1 s; 'connection reset' 15.0 vs 8.0 (RegExp wins).
RegExp runs in its own worker because a backtracking call can only be stopped by ending its worker; the page gives up after 10 s ('Native RegExp: more than 10 s.').

Simulating a set of automaton states in parallel avoids backtracking (Thompson, CACM 11(6), 1968; Russ Cox 2007); V8's Irregexp backtracks, and its linear-time engine was behind feature flags as of its 2021-01-11 blog post. The repo does not cite these; framing only.

The first json-search README (0732d26, 2026-10-13 09:01) said the GPU was 'clearly faster' for the highlighter half with documents staying on the GPU, already hedged; d79d9aa a minute later corrected three other sentences; the walk-back came from a review later that day, which found baselines on one of 18 cores and a second pass compared with a first.

The lab's answer to 'Is the GPU clearly faster?': against the same programs on the CPU yes (by 200 to 40,000 times); against RegExp on one thread faster back to back (1.5-9×) and on 7 of 10 patterns at a keystroke; against JavaScript in 8 workers no (RegExp 1.9-6.7 ms vs the GPU's 4.5-5.2 ms back to back, the GPU 2-8× as long after a pause).
A search after a 200 ms pause takes 2.4-3.2 times as long; a GPU lowering its clock would explain it but this is not verified, and keeping it busy didn't help.
